problem: End-to-end DRL navigation models are trained and tested on identical targets and scenes, so they degrade badly on unseen targets or environments. Image-specified goals also vary widely within a category, which further limits generalization.
motivation: Domestic robots need mapless visual navigation that adapts to new objects and rooms without retraining from scratch. The authors want to reuse prior navigation experience and adapt with only a few interactions, and to link goal and observation through semantics instead of raw appearance.
key_idea: Combine a text-goal, semantics-based siamese A3C navigation network (FCIS segmentation plus Word2vec) with a MAML-style meta-RL scheme that keeps updating parameters online in new scenes/targets.
insight: Semantic features and semantic word embeddings both matter: replacing FCIS+Word2vec with raw ResNet features (Our(vis)) or the word vectors with one-hot codes (Our(oh)) lowers success rate by about 27% and 36% respectively. Meta-adapting reaches convergence in about 50k steps in new scenes versus 300k-600k for retraining from scratch. Generalization is fragile: bathroom scenes never converged within a million steps, and unseen-target-plus-unseen-scene is the hardest scenario. Scene-type-specific models (Our(loc)) mostly beat the all-scene model (Our(glo)), which suggests overfitting.
method: Visual encoder: frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 on the four previous frames gives an 8192-d feature, then FC to 512-d.
FCIS semantic branch: frozen pre-trained FCIS produces per-pixel one-hot class maps (NMS IoU 0.3), then a 4-layer conv net to a 512-d feature.
Text target encoding: Word2vec (spaCy) 300-d word vector of the target class, then FC to 512-d, replacing the goal image of Zhu et al.
Fusion + A3C actor-critic: the 1536-d concatenation is fused to 512-d, then two FC layers give 3 policy logits and 1 value, trained with A3C and shared RMSProp (lr 7e-4).

MAML-style meta-training (Alg. 1): sample tasks (scene, target) from the training scenes, compute the policy-gradient loss on K=20 trajectories, take an inner gradient step to θ', resample with θ' and update θ; N=500 iterations.
Meta-adapting (Alg. 2): on test tasks, keep exploring and updating θ until convergence, with no rigid train/test boundary. SR/SPL are counted after 100 adaptation episodes.
Hyper-parameter search: a parallelizable grid search over N, α, β, tuned on the bathroom experiment, claimed to be cheaper than Bayesian optimization.

setting.backbone: ResNet50 (frozen) + FCIS (frozen) + Word2vec + A3C actor-critic (trained, MAML-adapted)
setting.training_data: Matterport3D scenes split into room areas (bedroom, bathroom, kitchen, living room); 5 scenes per type for training, 2 for testing; 3 target objects per type; RL from scratch with meta-training.
setting.observation: Monocular RGB frames (4 previous frames) plus text-defined target class; no depth
setting.action_space: Discrete low-level: move forward, turn left 30°, turn right 30°
setting.privileged: none (the Shortest Path baseline uses a map)

numbers_note: Table 1 (SPL and success rate per model, scenario and scene type) is referenced but its values are not in the extracted text, so no exact numbers are recorded. The text only gives approximate figures: Our(loc) SR about 30-40%, roughly 25% above GCN; Our(glo) best SR 42.1% in kitchen for scenario 2.
results: On Matterport3D room-level tasks, the MAML-based model (Our(loc), Our(glo)) outperforms Random, CVPR Target-Driven, MPSL, BRM and GCN in SPL and success rate across three generalization scenarios. Our(loc) reaches an average SR of 30-40%, about 25% above GCN. Adaptation converges in about 50k steps versus 300k-600k for retraining from scratch.
limitations: Poor generalization in some cases (bathroom never converged) and in the unseen-target-plus-unseen-scene scenario; performance is far below human level.
Small-scale evaluation (a few scenes per type, 3 targets per type, houses split into areas), with no depth and no comparison on standard benchmarks.
Needs many online adaptation episodes and interactions in the test scene, and hyper-parameter tuning.
